https://english.radio.cz/czech-prosecuto.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Czech prosecutors close probe into MP Turek's hate speech posts Facebook Twitter A police decision to drop an investigation into alleged hate speech by MP Filip Turek of the Motorists party is now legally binding, Prague prosecutors said on Monday. The supervising prosecutor said some of the social media posts did not constitute a criminal offence, while others did, but were published more than five years ago and are therefore barred by the statute of limitations. Police also concluded that Turek had authored the posts. The case concerns dozens of racist, sexist and other hateful comments on Turek's social media accounts, mainly Facebook, uncovered by Deník N after his election to parliament. The newspaper also highlighted repeated references to Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. Turek apologised for the remarks but denied writing some of the posts. https://ejewishphilanthropy.com/no-grave.text: Opinion A DEBT OWED No grave left unmarked By Harley Lippman August 20, 2026 Share Add EJP on Google In Short We are far less organized, and far less generous, in funding the work of finding our own dead. Forty-four years. That is how long IDF Sgt. First Class Yehuda Katz was missing. On June 11, 1982, his tank was overrun by Syrian forces in the Bekaa Valley, in one of the bloodiest engagements of the First Lebanon War. The crew was declared MIA. His two fellow soldiers from that battle, Zachary Baumel and Zvi Feldman, were eventually brought home, Baumel in 2019, Feldman last year. Katz remained the last unknown. This week, the IDF and Mossad announced that his remains have finally been located and identified, the end of a four-decade effort that outlasted multiple wars and the very regime that once held the intelligence. His family finally has a grave to visit. It is easy to read a headline like this and move on. It should not be moved past. It is a statement about who we are. Courtesy/Israel Defense Forces IDF Sgt. First Class Yehuda Katz. This year alone, the IDF’s Missing Persons Unit closed three more files from the War of Independence, now 78 years ago. Pvt. Dov Parmet, killed at 17 in 1948 near Malkia, was found in a mass grave after a six-year investigation combining archival research, soil analysis and archeological surveys. Pvt. Yaakov Zarihan, killed escorting a supply convoy to besieged Jerusalem, was located after 15 years of work. Shlomo Haimson, shot by British guards while trying to escape a Cyprus detention camp after learning of his daughter’s birth, was identified this month, his remains among those of more than 163 people brought to Israel in 1970, most buried in Haifa without identification. None of these men died in secret. Their families simply did not know where to stand and grieve. Israel decided, as a matter of state policy, that this was unacceptable, and built institutions whose sole purpose is to correct it, no matter how long it takes. The same instinct drove the more than two-year effort to bring home every hostage taken on Oct. 7, 2023, living and dead. When First Sgt. Ran Gvili’s remains were recovered from a Gaza cemetery this past January, the war’s darkest ledger finally closed. Israel had insisted, against pressure and fatigue and the passage of time, that “all of them” meant all of them, the murdered as much as the living, the last body as much as the first hostage released. I have spent decades engaged in a related, older and far larger version of this same work, in the forests and fields of Eastern Europe. The Holocaust is remembered, correctly, through Auschwitz, Treblinka and the other death camps. But hundreds of thousands of Jews were murdered outside the camps entirely, rounded up in their own towns and shot into pits in the woods, with no camp, no transport list and often no surviving witness. Many of those sites remain unmarked to this day, known only to a shrinking number of elderly local residents, if they are known at all. For decades, together with local Jewish organizations, Poland’s chief rabbi, historians, local officials and non-Jewish partners across the region, I have worked to identify these places, document them and see them properly marked. Not as a research project, but as a debt owed. Family and friends at the funeral of Ran Gvili, whose body was held by Hamas in the Gaza Strip since Oct. 7, 2023, and was returned to Israel in January 2026, in Meitar, southern Israel, Jan. 28, 2026. The parallel to Katz, to Parmet, to Gvili is not sentimental. It is structural. In every case, the work is the same: patient investigation, often taking years or decades; partnership with people, sometimes non-Jews, who hold a piece of the record; and a refusal to let time close the file. What differs is who is doing it. Israel has built standing institutions for this purpose and funds them permanently because it treats identifying its fallen as a core function of Jewish sovereignty, not a discretionary one. In the Diaspora, the equivalent work of locating and preserving the sites where Jews were murdered without record is carried out largely by a scattering of underfunded nonprofits and individual efforts like my own, without anything resembling that institutional backing. That gap should trouble Jewish philanthropy. We are generous funders of Jewish education, of Israel advocacy, of security for our institutions. We are far less organized, and far less generous, in funding the work of finding our own dead. There is no Diaspora equivalent of the IDF’s Genomic Center for Identifying Fallen Soldiers. There is no coordinated, well-resourced Diaspora institution whose job is to do for Holocaust-era mass graves what Israel’s investigators did for Dov Parmet: treat every unmarked site as an open case rather than a closed chapter. This is one of the instances in which the Diaspora has something clear to learn from Israel, rather than the reverse. Israel has shown, across 78 years and every war since, that a nation can decide, as policy, that no missing person is ever quietly written off; that the search continues after the headlines fade and the people who remember have themselves passed away. Jewish philanthropic institutions abroad should study that model and fund accordingly: endow the forensic and archival work; formalize partnerships with local governments and historians across Eastern Europe; and treat the last unmarked grave with the same seriousness Israel brought to the last missing tank crewman. Yehuda Katz is home. So is Ran Gvili. So, now, are Dov Parmet, Yaakov Zarihan and Shlomo Haimson, each one returned to memory after decades in the dark. Their families finally have a grave to visit, a place to recite the mourner’s Kadish . The work is never finished. But it continues because a people decided, as a matter of principle, that it must. That principle should not stop at Israel’s borders. Businessman and philanthropist Harley Lippman works to advance U.S .and Jewish interests around the globe, including the U.S. Commission for the Preservation of America’s Heritage Abroad, and has led efforts to find and preserve Jewish graves in Eastern Europe. https://www.dw.com/en/vanuatu-ferry-caps.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MWX4 The MV Matui sank Friday after leaving Santo Island, it never arrived at its destination, Ambae Island, some 96 kilometers to the east Image: Chris McCall/AFP Advertisement At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday. The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,900 miles) east of Australia . The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities. The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae. Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea." Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials. In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts ‌move ​toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors." "To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To ⁠the ​families of those missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," ​the statement continued. Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui. "This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel." Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized." French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted. It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor. "He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge. "There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added. Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own. The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort. A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning. The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning. Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Prisons and probation Prisoners to ‘double up’ in one-person prefab cells, leaked documents show Exclusive: Ten category C prisons in England and Wales asked to add second beds, in breach of safe occupancy limits Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.41 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Prison Service has drawn up plans to “double up” hundreds of prisoners in temporary prefabricated cells built for one person, at the request of the Ministry of Justice, leaked documents show. Amid an ongoing overcrowding crisis in England and Wales, governors of 10 category C prisons have been asked to sign off the installation of second beds in “rapid deployment cells [RDCs]”. The units, some of which measure 2.9 metres by 3.4 metres and include a bed, toilet and shower, were placed in the grounds of more than 15 prisons as a temporary solution to past overcrowding problems. Estimated to have a 15-year lifespan, the steel-framed “pods” can be stacked to be two storeys and are usually occupied by low-risk prisoners, some of whom have been allowed to move into them as a reward for good behaviour. According to leaked emails, the planned doubling-up suggested by Ministry of Justice officials would increase the overall capacity of the prison estate by 476. Responding to the leaked documents, governors and prison officers said the numbers being proposed by Whitehall could breach health and safety laws and make jails unsafe for prisoners, staff and the public. Map of prisons where ‘doubling up’ has been proposed The plans were disclosed in an email sent on 27 August by a senior Prison Service executive to governors. “As you are aware, maximising available prison capacity is of high ministerial interest, and HMPPS [His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service] have been asked to explore the viability of crowding Rapid Deployment Cell accommodation,” the executive wrote. “The physical viability of installing a second bed in these units has been worked through at pace, and the assessment … is that ground floor units only are suitable to install a second bed. “Given continued high population growth, and less supply coming online than anticipated, it is important that all potential capacity is identified quickly, and as such the panels need to take place over the next few days.” The email was sent three days before Andy Burnham announced a substantial narrowing of prisoners’ eligibility for the government’s early release scheme , blocking hundreds of violent criminals from being freed. What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why? Read more According to a second leaked document, the doubling up plans would include beds being added to temporary cells in the following prisons: Wayland, in Norfolk (43 beds); Littlehey, in Cambridgeshire (60); Erlestoke, in Wiltshire (66); and Rochester, in Kent (60). Other prisons asked to find extra capacity in temporary cells include The Verne, in Dorset; Wymott, in Lancashire; Channings Wood, in Devon; Whatton, in Nottingham, which is a prison for people convicted of sexual offences; The Mount, in Hertfordshire; and Huntercombe, in Oxfordshire. The second document also shows that the doubling up proposals would breach “operational capacity”, putting the number of prisoners above safe occupancy levels. Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers Association, said capacity breaches could prompt industrial action by his members. “By law our members cannot strike, but I know they would walk out on health and safety grounds if asked to oversee prisons which cannot cope with the numbers being proposed,” he said. “Creating more space increases the pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate and risks the stability of prisons. If the government are convinced that early release schemes are sufficient, you have to ask why they are now insisting prisons source every available bit of spare capacity.” Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors Association, said a full risk assessment would have to be carried out on each prison to ensure the public and staff remained safe if doubling up occurred. “RDCs are amongst the least secure accommodation in the prison estate and prisoners located in them will have to be risk assessed. If you don’t do this, the prison won’t be sufficiently safe or secure,” he said. “Increasing the operational capacity of a prison isn’t as simple as putting bunk beds in cells. There needs to be staff available to supervise the additional prisoners and there needs to be additional regime activities.” Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the proposal was an act of desperation. “Rapid deployment cells were themselves meant to be a short-term response but, ironically, they have come to be seen as being among the more positive parts of the prison estate, with fewer issues related to violence, debt and drug misuse. The risk now is that all this will be undermined as more and more people get crammed in,” she said. There are 87,111 people in prison in England and Wales . Under the Ministry of Justice’s own definition of safety and decency, the prison estate should not hold more than 81,616 people. Reacting to the leaked documents, a ministry spokesperson said the department was investing up to £4.7bn creating 14,000 new prison places. “As the public would expect, we’re pulling every lever available to ensure there is always space to lock up dangerous offenders,” the spokesperson said. “Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so, and no final decision has been taken on these units.” Explore more on these topics Prisons and probation England Wales UK criminal justice news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Ministers propose converting female prison estate into cells for men What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why? https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: The Trump administration has widened its use of taxpayer-funded television advertisements promoting President Donald Trump, airing a second spot within three days and pushing spending on the first ad past $443,000.The White House has maintained that the ads are public service announcements, similar to those used by past presidents, but lawmakers from both parties criticised the first spot on Thursday, questioning its legality and appropriateness given its political tone, its timing so close to November's midterms and its use of taxpayer funds.Also read: 'Trump Strait': US President shares new map of Hormuz after rejecting Iran's 7-day ceasefire offerThe new, minute-long ad features scenic night-time visuals of Mount Rushmore layered with quotes and clips from Trump's Fourth of July weekend speech there marking the country's 250th anniversary. We know that this is not an ending. This is only the beginning of the golden age of America, Trump says in the ad, which closes with onscreen text reading, Paid for by the U.S. Government. The exact cost of the new ad was not immediately known, but it was airing on Newsmax on Friday, including slots on Carl Higbie Frontline and Greg Kelly Reports, according to media-spending tracker AdImpact.The first ad, a 30-second spot that began airing Wednesday, features clips of Trump speaking on defeating communism, layered with onscreen text promoting the largest tax cuts in history, reigniting American manufacturing and a call to defend law and order and police. The spot's soundtrack includes a chorus repeating love me and ends with the same government-funding disclosure.Defending the campaign on Friday, the White House said the ads were very clearly not campaign ads, noting that Trump is not on the ballot and that the ads carry no call to action. It cited past administrations of both parties buying network time for public service messaging, including the George W Bush administration's Medicare law campaign and the Biden administration's COVID-19 vaccination drive. Patriotism isn't partisan. These public service announcements are unapologetically American, clearly disclosed, and aimed at the country, not a line on the ballot, the White House said. It did not respond to a query on which part of the government had supplied the funds.Also read: Trump said he would campaign in midterm battlegrounds. He's starting in deep red states insteadLawmakers from both parties criticised the ads on Thursday, with some pointing out that federal law bars the use of taxpayer funds for publicity or propaganda and restricts partisan political activity by government employees. Notably, Republicans defending their congressional majorities in the midterms have themselves run ads carrying similar messaging on communism, the economy and crime.Several senior House Democrats demanded on Thursday that the first ad be pulled off air, calling it the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea. North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who is not seeking re-election, called the ad inappropriate and compared it to messaging he would expect from former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban. (With inputs from AP)

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/10/17/andr.text: Menü Kereső Andrej Babiš a szenátusi választásról: Ez az eredmény katasztrófa Külföld Ignácz Péter Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Katasztrofálisnak nevezte a szenátusi választás eredményét a kormánykoalíciós Elégedetlen Polgárok Akciója (ANO) párt számára Andrej Babiš pártelnök, cseh kormányfő szombaton Prágában újságírók előtt. A részleges szenátusi választást, amelyen a 81 tagú szenátus egyharmada, tehát 27 mandátum újult meg, elsöprő ellenzéki győzelem született. Az ANO jelöltjei, bár 13 esetben bejutottak a második fordulóba, egyetlen mandátumot sem tudtak szerezni. „Az ANO mozgalom számára ez az eredmény katasztrófa. Azt biztosan nem gondoltuk, hogy ezen a választáson egyetlen mandátumot sem szerzünk. Sajnos minden úgy végződött, ahogy végződött” – mondta Babiš a pártközpontban tartott sajtótájékoztatón, miután ismertté váltak a pénteken és szombaton tartott második választási forduló eredményei. A kormányfő szerint a választás eredménye nem lesz hatással a kormány stratégiájára, abban nem lesz változás. „Semmiféle stratégiaváltás nincs napirenden” – hangsúlyozta. A koalíció januárban újra értékeli az eddigi munkát, majd folytatja a kormányprogram teljesítését – jegyezte meg. Hazugságnak nevezte azokat a sajtóban megjelent ellenzéki állításokat, miszerint a kabinet nem teljesíti a kormányprogramot. Pártként a választás győztese az ellenzéki Polgármesterek és Függetlenek (STAN), amely tíz mandátumot szerzett. A Polgári Demokratikus Párt (ODS) hét, a kereszténydemokrata KDU-CSL három, a TOP 09 két mandátumot mondhat magáénak, további öt mandátum a különböző helyi koalícióké. Az ellenzéki Kalózpárt eddigi egyetlen mandátumát elveszítette. A szenátusi választás eredménye – vélekedett a pártelnök – egyértelműen a regionális szervezetek hibája. „Úgy vélem, el kell gondolkodnunk azon, hogy miért és hogyan történt, ami történt. El kell gondolkodni azon, hogy a mozgalomban ki az, aki valóban dolgozik és ki nem, ki az, aki csak az erős márkanévre számít, ki az, aki kisajátította a regionális szervezeteket” – jelentette ki. „Észrevettem: sok embernek az az érzése, hogy ha az ANO tagja, akkor az biztos győzelmet jelent” – tette hozzá.
